questions.statement: She ___ already finished her homework. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: A student is checking her homework before the class starts.

options.feedback: Has is correct: the third person singular she takes has plus the past participle finished.
Have is used with I, you, we and they, but the subject she needs has.
Had is the past perfect and would point to an action before another past action, not to this present result.
Having is a participle and cannot act as the finite auxiliary of this sentence.

questions.explanation:
With the subject she the present perfect auxiliary is has, so the sentence reads she has already finished. Already signals that the result matters now.

questions.statement: When we arrived at the cinema, the film ___ already started. Choose the correct form.
questions.context: Two friends talk about a film they missed yesterday.

options.feedback: Has is present perfect and cannot order two events that both lie in the past.

Have is the plural present perfect and does not fit the singular subject the film.
Was cannot carry the past participle started in this construction.

questions.explanation:
The film started before we arrived, and both events are past. The earlier action takes the past perfect: had started.

Have is correct: the first person I takes have in the present perfect.
Am is the verb be and cannot be followed by the past participle been.

options.text: We had finished the project before the deadline.

options.feedback: This is incorrect: the present perfect cannot be used with a finished past date such as yesterday.

options.text: We have finished the project already.
options.feedback: This is correct English: already can accompany the present perfect to show completion.

The present perfect never takes a finished past time marker. Yesterday demands the past simple, so the first sentence is wrong.
